paras: The New Orleans riverfront lockout violence of September 16, 1903, was a series of confrontations in which striking longshoremen drove Black longshoremen from a wharf and white union men threatened to lynch J. B. Williams, president of the colored longshoremen's union. Police broke up the crowd at the wharf after a riot call, and no injuries were reported.

A ten-day longshoremen's strike that had tied up the port ended in mid-September with an agreement to be signed for three years. On September 16 the steamship companies locked out all union men on the riverfront, citing an alleged violation of that settlement, and nearly all ocean shipping at the port stopped.

That morning, at the wharf where the coffee ship Canaries was being unloaded, some Black longshoremen who were "not pleased with the action of the unions" tried to go to work, and a crowd of strikers drove them from the docks. When police interfered, the strikers threatened to throw officers, agents and reporters into the river, and strike committee chairman Moriarity urged them to buy Winchesters and shotguns and hold the wharves by force. A large force of police answered a riot call and dispersed the strikers.

Later that day a crowd of white union men denounced the executive committee of the colored longshoremen's union, whose members fled to escape a beating. White longshoremen also threatened to lynch Williams, and according to the dispatch the threats led Black workers to rally to his support.

No arrests were reported. On October 7, when Williams went to the Harrison liner Orion to see whether union men were working there, he was "forcibly ejected and sent across the river"; the report does not say by whom.

The only account of the September 16 violence found is a telegraph dispatch in the New-York Tribune, headlined "New-Orleans Shipping Tied Up," which treated the attacks as part of a labor dispute and described a "riotous scene" without comment. It named the division between white and colored unions but presented the Black workers as dissenters from union policy; no Black-press account of the violence was found. The Bryan Morning Eagle in Texas later carried a brief report of Williams's ejection from the Orion.

accounts.label: Telegraph report from New Orleans
accounts.gist: Black longshoremen unhappy with the unions' action tried to work and were driven off by strikers; police dispersed the crowd after a riot call, and later white union men drove off the colored union's committee and threatened to lynch Williams, which rallied Black workers to him.

framing.detail: The Tribune headlined the shipping tie-up and lockout ("New-Orleans Shipping Tied Up"), describing a "riotous scene" and union factionalism without editorial comment.
The only Black-press item found, a Savannah Tribune digest line, noted only that the strike had been concluded with a three-year agreement and did not mention the violence.

A crowd of strikers (race not stated) drove off the Black workers; a crowd of white union men denounced the colored union's executive committee and white longshoremen threatened to lynch Williams

sources.note: Telegraph report dated Sept. 16: strikers drove Black longshoremen from the Canaries wharf; riot call; white union men drove off the colored union's executive committee and threatened to lynch union president J. B. Williams.
quotes: There was a riotous scene this morning at the wharf where the coffee ship Canaries is being unloaded.
Some of the negro longshoremen were not pleased with the action of the unions and attempted to go to work, when a crowd of strikers appeared and drove them from the docks.
Threats were made by union men to lynch J. B. Williams, the president of the colored longshoremen's union.
These threats were made by white longshoremen, and had the effect of causing the negroes to rally to the support of their chief.

set_aside: Fourteen Black men brought from Texas to replace Southern Pacific freight handlers fled after a motorman warned they would be killed at the docks; a separate strike.
Brevity that New Orleans longshoremen had gone on another strike, claiming their leaders betrayed them; no violence or race mentioned.
